newsitem.title: UK: UK consumers ambivalent on gene foods, study says.
newsitem.headline: UK consumers ambivalent on gene foods, study says.

text.p: UK consumers are ambivalent about the use of genetically modified organisms (GMOs) in food products, according to an academic study.
The study, "Uncertain World - Genetically Modified Organisms, Food and Public Attitudes in Britain," comes from the Centre for the Study of Environmental Change at the University of Lancaster.
It is based on collaboration between the university, Unilever Plc and the environmentalist Green Alliance, Unilever said in a statement.
"The report has uncovered a disturbing degree of latent public unease about genetically modified foods in Britain".

"What is more, key public concerns revealed by the research are being neglected, systematically, by the existing political and regulatory framework," Robin Grove-White, one of the report's co-authors, is quoted as saying.
"This throws a major challenge to industry and government," he said.
A variety of products were referred to in the study, including genetically modified tomatoes, which are already on sale in the UK.

Others included cheese manufactured using genetic techniques, as well as Roundup ready, a gene-modified soy developed by Monsanto Co in the U.S., and a gene maize produced by Swiss chemicals group Ciba Geigy AG.

The report highlights a sense of inevitability and fatalism about the possible future pervasiveness of GMOs in foods. Paradoxically, people may purchase particular GMO products, whilst also feeling uneasy about the technology as a whole, it says.
It reflects "the reality that much such unease is currently latent rather than explicit," Unilever's statement says.
People have mixed feelings about the integrity and adequacy of present patterns of government regulation and in particular about official scientific assurances of safety.
It refers to the role of the BSE crisis in "compounding latent public unease about the limits of expert knowledge, both generally and in relation to GMO possibilities specifically."
The report urges a two year programme of institutional experiments aimed at a greater involvement of the public.

It seeks "to develop more socially resilient shared understandings of the conditions of acceptability or otherwise of GMO foods and ...improve the 'social intelligence' of industry and government vis a vis relevant public sensibilities and concerns".

It also urges "recognition that while full labelling of GMO products is regarded by many informed bodies as a necessary condition for proper market regulation, it is still not a sufficient condition for addressing some of the most important public concerns identified in the research."
